claims.statement: AFIR distinguishes private points restricted to a limited and determinate group from publicly accessible points, while a point on private property accessible to a general group such as customers can still be publicly accessible.

AFIR recognizes private depots and logistics centres as important locations for overnight and destination charging of heavy-duty electric vehicles and requires smart, digital capabilities for covered public infrastructure.
Hypothesis: owners will license predictable off-hours slots and fleets will subscribe rather than build capacity; host supply, fleet willingness and unit utilization are unvalidated.

contrary_evidence: Public accessibility can bring ad-hoc payment, price, data, uptime and API obligations, reducing the simplicity of the private-host thesis.
AFIR's recognition of private depots supports the use case but does not show that third-party hosts have spare capacity or lawful resale rights.

economics.acquisition_route: Pre-sell 20 fleet slots in one micro-market, then contract five existing chargers within route distance; use manual booking before integrating hardware.
economics.founder_net_worth_path: Unvalidated path: 2,500 subscribed slots at PLN 250 monthly platform revenue after energy pass-through would produce PLN 7.5m annual revenue; at 25% operating profit and a 4x value, a 70% founder stake would be about PLN 5.25m. A 7-9 year route requires multi-city density and low churn, not merely signed hosts.
economics.founder_time: 12-18 hours per week for site contracting, compliance, scheduling and exception response; a local operator is needed once sessions become daily.
economics.gross_margin_basis: Unvalidated estimate: 35-55% after host payments, payment processing, support and light access-control retrofits; electricity is a pass-through and major grid upgrades are excluded.
economics.payback: Unvalidated target: 15-24 months at 150-250 reserved vehicle slots, assuming no grid-upgrade funding and positive host-level contribution.
economics.pricing: Unvalidated hypothesis: PLN 300-800 per reserved vehicle slot monthly plus a PLN 0.20-0.50/kWh service margin or PLN 12-25 session fee, with transparent host revenue share.
economics.retention_or_repeat: Fleets renew while slots are dependable and cheaper than alternative depot capex; hosts renew while utilization revenue exceeds access inconvenience.

fingerprint.compounding_advantage: dense clusters of exclusive time windows, utilization history and reliable host operations improve route usefulness and raise switching costs for fleets
fingerprint.customer: small commercial fleets that need dependable overnight charging without building a depot, with private charger owners as capacity suppliers
fingerprint.distribution_mechanism: fleet-leasing firms and local business associations recruit demand while electrical and renewable installers identify technically suitable host sites
fingerprint.offer_and_business_model: contracted off-hours access, booking, remote unlock or key control, usage reconciliation and support sold as a recurring capacity subscription
fingerprint.payer_and_paid_event: fleets pay a monthly reserved-slot fee plus metered charging/service charges; hosts receive agreed energy reimbursement and revenue share after a completed session
fingerprint.problem_trigger: fleet electrification, a depot lease without enough power, charger downtime, or a host seeking revenue from idle equipment

founder_fit: Renewable-installation relationships can identify charger hosts and technical partners.
Scheduling, pricing and utilization optimization fit the founder's data background.
A manual, single-cluster pilot limits capital before hardware integration.
Partner-led fleet acquisition avoids a consumer influencer model.
risks: Opening a private-property charger to a broad user group may make it publicly accessible and trigger AFIR payment, data and operational duties.
Landlord, parking, fire, insurance or electricity-resale constraints may block host contracts.
Old chargers may lack remote control or reliable metering.
Low geographic density or unreliable host access can make reserved slots operationally useless.

structure.control_point: contracted charging, parking and entry slots at private sites during otherwise idle hours, concentrated into fleet-usable geographic clusters
structure.critical_dependency: host property and electricity arrangements must permit the service, chargers must interoperate with access and billing, and local fleet demand must produce adequate utilization

thesis: Acquire defined nighttime and weekend operating licences from owners of underused workplace, hotel and commercial EV chargers, then sell reserved charging-and-parking capacity to local delivery, service and taxi fleets. Hosts keep ownership and receive energy reimbursement plus revenue share; the platform controls only contracted time windows, access rules and booking. Validate one dense Warsaw or Wielkopolska corridor before any hardware rollout, and treat a site as publicly accessible only after legal classification and AFIR compliance review.
title: Off-Hours Private Charger Capacity Network
uncertainties: How much recurring fleet demand exists in a single reachable micro-market?
What contractual definition keeps a limited fleet group private, and when is public-access compliance preferable?
Which installed charger models can support low-cost metering and access control?
What minimum host payment secures genuinely reserved slots rather than best-effort access?
